analysis.one_liner: Strengthens federal penalties and tools for workers to recover wages their employers never paid them.
analysis.headline: The bill was introduced with 14 Senate cosponsors and referred to the Senate labor committee, which never acted on it before Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill targets wage theft—employers not paying minimum wage, skipping overtime, requiring off-the-clock work, or withholding final paychecks. It would require employers to give workers paystubs and written pay terms, let workers see their payroll records, force employers to pay what a contract promises rather than just the minimum wage, double the damages workers can recover, ban forced arbitration of wage claims, extend the time limit for suing, and fund $50 million a year in grants for worker outreach and enforcement partnerships.
analysis.who_benefits: Workers whose employers underpay them—especially low-wage workers in restaurants, retail, construction, janitorial work, and home care, where studies cited in the bill found violations are common. The bill's findings note women, immigrants, and Black workers experience minimum wage violations at higher rates [S3]. Workers would gain paystubs showing how pay was calculated, the right to inspect up to five years of payroll records, the contractually promised wage rate, double the current damages plus interest, longer to sue (four to five years instead of two to three), and the right to take wage claims to court rather than forced arbitration [S2][S3].

how_it_helps.text: Requires employers to give new hires written pay terms and every worker itemized paystubs showing hours, rates, overtime, and deductions, so workers can see when they are being shorted [S2][S3].
Doubles the damages employers must pay for minimum wage and overtime violations, adds interest, and triples damages for retaliating against workers who complain [S2][S3].
Bars employers from making workers sign away their right to sue over wages as a condition of employment or in a pre-dispute arbitration agreement [S2][S3].
Extends the deadline for wage lawsuits from two or three years to four or five, and stops the clock while the Labor Department investigates [S2][S3].
Gives workers the right to their full contractually agreed wage, not just the legal minimum, and requires final pay within 14 days of leaving a job [S2][S3].
Authorizes $50 million a year through 2020 in grants for nonprofits, unions, and community groups to educate workers, help file claims, and partner with Labor Department enforcement [S3].

analysis.who_pays: Employers, especially those in industries with high rates of wage violations, would pay more in back wages, doubled damages, interest, and fines up to $10,000 per affected employee for repeat violations, and could face mandatory Justice Department referral for willful offenses like falsifying records [S3]. Law-abiding employers would bear new administrative costs for paystubs, disclosures, and record requests [S3].

drawbacks.text: Employers would face sharply higher exposure—double damages plus interest, fines up to $10,000 per employee for willful or repeat violations, and a rebuttable presumption against them if they cannot produce complete records—costs that small businesses in thin-margin industries argue are difficult to absorb and may be passed to consumers or reduced staffing [S3].

The bill adds new paperwork duties: written pay disclosures within 15 days of hiring, detailed itemized paystubs for every pay period, and copies of up to five years of records within 21 days of a worker's request, a real administrative burden for small employers [S3].

Mandatory referral of willful offenders to the Justice Department for prosecution, including criminal penalties of $10,000 per affected employee, is a much harsher enforcement posture than current practice, where criminal referral is rare [S3].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The costs fall mainly on employers who are not paying legally owed wages, and the bill's own findings cite DOL data that a third of employers caught stealing wages kept doing so because penalties were too low [S3]. The main real tradeoff is the compliance burden on small businesses and the risk that heavier litigation damages raise costs in low-margin industries. Weighing that against an estimated $8.6 billion a year taken from workers through wage violations, the benefits to working people substantially outweigh the compliance costs, though the damages multiplier and presumption rules would predictably generate more litigation.

outcome.mechanism: It was referred to the Senate labor committee the day it was introduced, and the committee never took it up before Congress ended, so it died without a hearing, a vote, or any action at all.

narrative.text: Senator Patty Murray introduced the bill in the Senate on March 16, 2016 [S1][S5].
The same day, it was read twice and referred to the Senate Health, Education, Labor, and Pensions Committee [S5].
Fourteen senators signed on as cosponsors—13 of the 44 Senate Democrats and 1 of the 2 Independents; no Republican cosponsored [S4].
No further action was ever taken: the committee held no markup and the bill never reached the Senate floor before the 114th Congress ended on January 3, 2017 [S1][S5].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Employers who underpay workers keep the current system, where penalties are low, arbitration waivers are enforceable, and workers have two to three years to sue. Workers whose wages were stolen received no new remedy.

for.name: Patty Murray
for.what_they_did: Sponsored the bill and introduced it in the Senate.

for.name: Sherrod Brown, Al Franken, Bernie Sanders, Elizabeth Warren, and other original cosponsors
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill alongside Murray as original cosponsors.

against.name: Lamar Alexander
against.role: Chair, Senate Health, Education, Labor, and Pensions Committee
against.what_they_did: Chair of the committee the bill was referred to; the committee never scheduled a markup or took any action on it, and it died there.

against.name: 54 of 54 Senate Republicans
against.what_they_did: No Republican sponsored or cosponsored the bill, leaving it with no path to a floor vote in a Republican-controlled Senate.

sides.party_line_note: Every sponsor and all 14 cosponsors were Democrats or the Independent who caucuses with them; no Republican signed on, and with Republicans holding 54 Senate seats and the committee chairmanship, the bill never moved.

industries.industry: Low-wage employers in high-violation industries (restaurants, retail, janitorial, home care, construction)
industries.note: These employers would face double damages plus interest, fines up to $10,000 per affected employee, mandatory criminal referral for willful record falsification, and a rebuttable presumption of liability when their records are incomplete [S3]. The bill's findings cite studies showing compliance below 50 percent in certain industries, which is exactly where the new penalties would bite hardest [S3].

industries.industry: Employers and the arbitration industry generally
industries.note: The bill bars requiring workers to waive their right to court— including class and collective actions—as a condition of employment or in a pre-dispute arbitration agreement, removing a widely used tool for keeping wage disputes out of court [S2][S3].

industries.industry: Worker advocacy groups, legal aid organizations, and labor unions
industries.note: They would be eligible for a new $50-million-a-year grant program to educate workers about their rights, help them file claims, and partner with the Labor Department on enforcement [S3].

The bill's findings argue honest employers are at a competitive disadvantage against wage violators, so stronger enforcement levels the field, but they also bear new paystub, disclosure, and recordkeeping compliance costs [S3].
